title: File organisations and index types
lead: Finding one student, finding every match and inserting a new record require different page work. Derive the costs before choosing a file or index.
goals: Compare heap and sorted-file costs under the same assumptions
Distinguish a search key, a primary key, and an index entry
Calculate the data-fetch costs of clustered and unclustered indexes

sections.title: Find one student, then try to find every match
sections.html:
Imagine student records on four pages. In this original teaching file the student IDs are P1=[2,8], P2=[1,6], P3=[7,3], P4=[10,5]. We want ID 7. Read P1: no match. Read P2: no match. Read P3: found it. Because ID is unique, stop. If the question were “find every student aged 20”, finding one student would not justify stopping; another page could contain another match. Without useful ordering or an index, every page must be checked. A file with no required search-key order is a heap file.

Now arrange these same IDs in order: [1,2], [3,5], [6,7], [8,10]. For a range 3–7, first locate where 3 could begin, then scan right through 3,5,6,7 and stop when 8 exceeds the range. This is a sorted file. To locate a starting region, inspect a middle page and discard the half that cannot contain the key; repeating this is binary search. It works because page ranges follow the search order. Sorting by ID provides no such guarantee when searching by age.

But inserting ID 4 into the compact sorted sequence means making room before 5, potentially moving later records. In the heap, we can append to a known page with spare room. We have uncovered the trade-off before calculating it: ordering helps selective lookups and ranges, while maintaining compact order makes changes expensive. An index will offer a separate lookup structure; it does not make reading the full table free.

Scope source: Lecture 8, physical PDF pages 2–19. Open source. The numerical examples and scenarios here are original teaching material, not slide figures or measured data.

sections.title: Derive the page costs from the work
sections.html:
Use the lecture’s simplified model: P data pages, R records per page, D time per read or write. Ignore CPU, caching, prefetching, and random/sequential differences. For our original numerical exercise, P=1024 and D=2 ms. The sought unique key exists and is equally likely to lie on any page. Heap insertion knows a final page with spare space; sorted storage is compact with no reserved gaps. These assumptions matter to every number below.

OperationCount the workEstimated time
Read all recordsRead P pages, for either layout1024×2=2048 ms
Heap: existing unique keyRead 1…P pages according to its location; average (P+1)/2512.5×2=1025 ms (≈1024 ms in P/2 model)
Sorted: key on sorting attributeHalve 1024 candidate pages about 10 timeslog₂1024×2=20 ms, approximate
Heap: insertRead last page; change it; write it2×2=4 ms
Compact sorted: insert/deleteLocate position; shift about P/2 pages, each read and written(10+2×512)×2=2068 ms

A heap miss differs from a successful unique-key lookup: absence is established only after all P pages, so it costs PD. The same full scan is needed for nonunique equality or a range when no suitable access path exists. Heap deletion first finds the row, then writes its changed page: approximately (P/2+1)D=1026 ms in the half-file model. A known RID, a cached page or a different free-space policy changes these counts.

In a sorted file, finding a starting position does not retrieve every matching page. If K additional matching-region pages are charged by the model, use (log₂P+K)D. For K=4 that is (10+4)×2=28 ms. State how the first matching page is counted; overlap can refine this approximation. The 20 ms estimate compares simplified organisations and is not a real elapsed-time measurement.

Why is the heap cost for an absent unique ID larger than its successful average?

Reasoned answer. A successful search can stop when uniqueness proves no other match is needed. No page seen so far proves absence from unseen heap pages, so a miss scans to the end.

Key takeaway

Binary search requires the file to follow the search order. A file sorted by product code does not support binary search by price. The logarithmic cost below applies only when the search condition matches the sorting column.

Scope source: Lecture 8, physical PDF pages 5–19. Open source. The numerical examples and scenarios here are original teaching material, not slide figures or measured data.

sections.title: Follow an index entry all the way to the record
sections.html:
Return to Product(pid,category,price): (1,tea,20), (2,tea,25), (3,cake,30). Looking up category=tea must find two records even though pid is unique. The indexed attribute category is the search key; “key” here does not promise uniqueness. Suppose the two tea rows have RIDs P3/slot1 and P8/slot2. A RID, record identifier, tells us the page and slot to fetch; it does not contain the product price.

Entry representationWhat tea storesHow to get price
A: whole record(tea, complete product record)Read it from the entry
B: one reference per row(tea,P3/1), (tea,P8/2)Fetch both referenced records
C: reference list per value(tea,[P3/1,P8/2])Fetch both referenced records

B and C allow several indexes to reference the same stored record. C reduces repeated key entries for duplicates, but its lists vary in length. The representation is independent of whether the lookup structure is a tree or a hash table. A tree preserves key order for ranges; hashing maps equal keys to a bucket but does not preserve range order.

Now hold the lookup result fixed at 80 qualifying records. At 20 records per page, matches packed on four pages cost four data-page reads from a cold cache. If every match lies on a different page, they can cost 80. The first arrangement illustrates clustering: nearby search-key values reside near one another physically. An unclustered tree still orders its index entries correctly; it is the subsequent data fetch that is scattered. Add index-path and leaf reads to these four or 80 reads. One physical file generally has only one independent clustering order, and maintaining it costs space and update work.

Keep the remaining labels separate. A candidate key is a minimal attribute set guaranteed unique; the primary key is one chosen candidate. In these slides, a primary index has a search key containing the primary key; a unique index has a search key containing a candidate key. The slides describe a secondary index as using a search key that may match multiple records. These course conventions do not determine clustering and may differ from product terminology.

Key takeaway

Add the cost of locating index entries to the cost of fetching records. The four or 80 reads above count only data pages. Also count the path through the index and the leaf pages containing its entries when those pages are not already cached.

Scope source: Lecture 8, physical PDF pages 20–34. Open source. The numerical examples and scenarios here are original teaching material, not slide figures or measured data.

sections.title: Choose against a workload, not a label
sections.html:
A design decision starts with the operation that repeats. For a nightly export of every row, both heap and sorted files read P pages; sorting may be valuable only if the consumer needs that order. For frequent single-code lookups and updates, an equality-capable index can narrow the reads, but each indexed change also maintains the index. For date-range reports returning many neighbouring dates, an ordered tree and useful clustering can reduce scattered record fetches; maintaining physical order may make inserts harder. No design is free across all three workloads.

A table has a tree on date. A query matches 80 rows, but the rows are spread over 80 cold data pages. A second organisation places them on four pages. Is “both use a tree” enough to predict equal cost?

Reasoned answer. No. Both may use similar index navigation, but the data-fetch portions are 80 versus four page reads under these assumptions. Check matching-page count, cache, required columns and maintenance workload. The fraction of matching rows, called selectivity, helps describe the request but does not alone determine the number of data pages.

If the request changes from one date to all dates, which earlier argument must be revisited?

Reasoned answer. The index no longer skips a selective region of the table. Traversing entries and then fetching the whole table may add overhead; compare a scan. Conversely, if the index contains every requested field, the data-fetch step may disappear. Access methods will examine these choices in detail.

Scope source: Lecture 8, physical PDF pages 20–34. Open source. The numerical examples and scenarios here are original teaching material, not slide figures or measured data.

quiz.question: The 80 matching records occupy four data pages. How many page reads fetch those records if none of the pages is cached?
quiz.explanation: Fetch each of the four required data pages once; all 80 matching records are on those pages. Several matching records share a page, so record count is not page-read count. This excludes the separately charged index path and assumes the pages are not cached.
